title: Projected stochastic momentum methods for nonlinear equality-constrained optimization for machine learning
contribution: Heavy-ball and Adam extensions of stochastic Newton-SQP for nonlinear equality constraints, with momentum taken over null-space-projected gradients, O(1/K)-to-noise-floor guarantees modelled on Defossez et al., and physics-informed learning experiments where projected Adam beats soft-constrained and projection-less Adam.
problem_entry: Momentum methods dominate unconstrained ML; the stochastic SQP of Berahas-Curtis-Robinson-Zhou has none; a prior constrained Adam lacks guarantees and averages raw gradients (pp. 2-3, 5).
key_idea: Split the step into a normal component and a null-space component and apply the momentum/Adam averages to P_k g_k, re-projecting the average, so J_k d_k = -rho_k c_k whatever the momentum (pp. 5, 9, 11).
assumptions: Stochastic objective, deterministic C1 constraints; on a set containing the iterates: bounded f below, bounded c, grad f, J, Lipschitz grad f and J, sigma_min(J) >= sigma_min (LICQ); unbiased projected gradient with bounded variance; bounded ||u_k||_inf for Adam (pp. 3, 5-6, 11).
proof_devices: Lipschitz continuity of P(x)grad f(x) via pseudoinverse algebra, Lemma 3.1 (p. 6)
analysis-only l1 merit phi = tau f + ||c||_1 with one-step bound (13) (p. 7)
geometric unrolling of momentum and Jensen on normalized weights, Lemma 3.4 (p. 7)
fresh-gradient / stale-drift / constraint split of grad f^T d with i-dependent Young weights, Lemma 3.5 (pp. 8-9)
orthogonality of normal and projected components to separate ||d||^2 (pp. 8, 10)
fixed tau chosen by (21) so objective and constraint coefficients coincide, Theorem 3.1 (p. 10)
Adam analysis borrowed term by term from Defossez et al. with modified bias correction and ordered parameter choice beta2 -> alpha -> K, Theorem 3.2 (pp. 11-18)
experiments: Four physics-informed problems (spring, 1-butene ODE, Burgers MLP; Darcy FNO) with 3-50 hard constraints; SQP-Heavyball, SQP-Adam vs soft-constrained Adam and projection-less Adam on the same objective; two learning rates each; mini-batch mean +- std over 5 runs; Burgers tie with Adam(unc) and poor heavy-ball printed (pp. 20-24).
positioning: Extends his own stochastic SQP [2] and models the analysis on Defossez et al. [10]; distinguishes from Marquez-Neila et al. [21] and O'Neill's Adagrad-type SQP [24]; hard constraints at training time vs soft constraints and constraint-embedding layers (pp. 2-3, 19).
writing: Priority claim ('first paper'), contribution ranked by practical performance, a reading paragraph after each theorem, hedged scale claims ending in a conjecture about larger networks (pp. 3, 11, 18-19, 24).
limits_future: Non-vanishing alpha*C/tau floor; assumptions on the iterates; small networks, two learning rates, 5 runs; only future direction is the conjecture that gains carry to larger networks (pp. 11, 19-24).

method_links.note: Same objective for all methods 'to ensure a fair comparison'; incumbent tie and heavy-ball failure printed; but only two learning rates and no rival tuning protocol.

No steering: merit parameter fixed by constants in the analysis, no merit line search, balance set by user-chosen rho_min and h_max; methodology explicitly avoids penalty/augmented-Lagrangian solves (Tension 3).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Momentum and Adam moments are taken over null-space-projected stochastic gradients and re-projected, leaving the linearized constraint step exact; called critical theoretically and practically.

transferable: Average P_k g_k rather than g_k when adding momentum or Adam to an equality-constrained method, keeping the normal step separate (pp. 5, 9).
Choose an analysis-only merit parameter so that the objective and constraint coefficients in the summed descent bound coincide (p. 10).
Model a constrained analysis line by line on a clean unconstrained proof and cite each reused lemma (pp. 12-13).
For hard-vs-soft constrained training comparisons, give all methods the identical objective and let the constrained ones only add constraints (p. 20).
coauthors: Qi Wang, Christian Piermarini, Yunlang Zhu

quotes.text: A critical feature of each extension is that the momentum terms are implemented with projected gradient estimates, rather than with the gradient estimates themselves.
Another key feature of this methodology is that one does not solve the hard-constrained training problem with a penalty-based (e.g., augmented Lagrangian) method.

title: A Local-Linearly Convergent Algorithm for Nonconvex Equality-Constrained Optimization
contribution: Shows that the Gradient-Eigenstep method on Fletcher's augmented Lagrangian reduces to linearly convergent gradient descent near strong second-order points, and uses this to prove that progressive sampling needs only N log(1/eps) full-sample gradient work in its epsilon-dependent term, versus O(N max{eps^-2, zeta^-3}) for a direct solve.
problem_entry: Fletcher's AL is exact and smooth and Goyens-Eftekhari-Boumal's method has global second-order complexity, but its local behaviour was unknown; that local rate is what the authors' progressive-sampling scheme needs (pp. 2-3, 14).
key_idea: With small fixed step and penalty above a threshold, the eigenstep branch never fires and the line search accepts the fixed step, so the method is gradient descent on F_rho with a linear rate; warm-started sampled stages then cost only logarithmically in eps (pp. 9-14, 24-25).
assumptions: C2 f and c; compact sublevel set of ||c||; Jacobian singular values bounded below near it; Lipschitz Hessians of f + c^T y and ||c||^2; start near a strong second-order point, rho > rho_beta, small eps and t; for sampling, uniform bounds over subsamples, bounded sample variances and a strongly Morse full problem (pp. 4-5, 9, 15-16).
proof_devices: Hessian of Fletcher's AL decomposed into null/range projections after differentiating the least-squares multiplier normal equations, giving separate curvature conditions, Lemma 2.1 (pp. 5-8)
three-invariant induction (iterate in C_R, gradient contraction, eigenvalue lower bound via Weyl-type perturbation) (pp. 10-12)
verification that the eigenstep test never fires and the Armijo test accepts the fixed step, so the algorithm reduces to gradient descent (pp. 13-14)
check of the cited method's assumptions A1-A5 one by one for sampled problems, Lemma 3.1 (pp. 17-18)
sign argument: strong Morse |d^T H d| >= beta plus approximate second-order stationarity gives d^T H d >= beta', Lemma 3.3 (pp. 19-22)
projection perturbation bounds from Stewart (p. 21)
monotonicity of the tolerance function in (b, kappa, rho) to obtain one uniform parameter interval, Lemma 3.4 (pp. 23-24)
geometric sum of per-stage sample costs, Theorem 3.1 (pp. 24-27)
experiments: none (theoretical; data statement p. 27; practical evidence delegated to [1], p. 22).
positioning: Fletcher, Di Pillo-Grippo, Estrin-Friedlander-Orban-Saunders, Goyens-Eftekhari-Boumal; extends another group's algorithm rather than proposing a rival and completes the authors' own progressive-sampling paper [1] (pp. 3, 14, 16).
writing: Twofold contribution repeated in abstract, introduction and conclusion; intuition paragraph on why rho must be large in the range space; explicit hedge that worst-case parameter rules are not needed in practice; performance measure justified before the theorem (pp. 2-3, 9, 22, 24, 27).
limits_future: Local start required; thresholds depend on unknown constants; global strong-Morse assumption; no experiments; no future directions stated (pp. 9, 16, 22-23, 27).

method_links.note: Penalty parameter fixed above an assumed threshold or chosen in an interval; no update rule designed; builds on a smooth exact augmented Lagrangian (Tension 3).

Measure (individual gradient/Jacobian evaluations) stated and justified and worst-case parameter rules disowned for practice, yet a worst-case complexity gain is produced without measurement (Tension 1).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A local-linear rate for an existing global-complexity method turns warm-started progressive-sampling stages into a bound whose eps-dependent term is N log(1/eps).
Extends the analysis of Goyens-Eftekhari-Boumal's Gradient-Eigenstep method instead of proposing a new method.

transferable: Decompose a penalty-function Hessian into null-space and range-space blocks to read off separate curvature conditions (pp. 7-8).
Prove that a complex method reduces to a simple one locally by verifying each branch test and line-search acceptance at the simple step (pp. 13-14).
Use strong Morse plus approximate second-order stationarity to upgrade curvature lower bounds via a sign argument (pp. 21-22).
Tie all per-stage tolerances and step sizes to one parameter mu in (0,1) so no stage is solved disproportionately tightly (p. 22).

quotes.text: In this case, the algorithm reduces to a gradient descent algorithm applied to minimize Fletcher’s augmented Lagrangian.
We emphasize, however, that for good practical performance, we do not expect these parameter requirements to be absolutely necessary.

title: NonOpt: Nonconvex, Nonsmooth Optimizer
contribution: Software paper (read as arXiv v1 / COR@L TR 25T-005) for NonOpt 2.0, a C++ framework unifying gradient sampling and proximal bundle with quasi-Newton models, adding a tailored predictor-corrector interior-point solver for the dual QP subproblems, with NonOpt-only experiments on synthetic QPs, 20 scalable test problems and large image denoising.
problem_entry: Consolidate a decade of nonsmooth algorithms into one extensible open-source code; no other actively developed open-source general-purpose locally Lipschitz solver is known (pp. 2-3, 14).
key_idea: One piecewise-quadratic model in an infinity-norm trust region covers both gradient sampling and bundle (only the point set differs), solved through its dual QP by a dual active-set or a new Mehrotra/Curtis-Nocedal interior-point solver chosen by subproblem size (pp. 5-6, 9-13, 17).
assumptions: f locally Lipschitz on the interior of its domain for well-definedness; guarantees need real-valued f plus C1 on a full-measure open set (GS) or weak upper semismoothness (bundle); gradient strategy has no general guarantee (pp. 3-4, 8).
proof_devices: no new theorems; guarantees cited (p. 4)
primal step recovered uniquely from a non-unique dual solution, d = -W(G omega + gamma) (pp. 5-6)
splitting gamma into positive and negative parts to get a standard-form QP (pp. 9-10)
G omega as approximate minimum-norm Clarke subgradient, with Caratheodory's n+1 bound explaining why exact stationarity tests are too costly (p. 18)
experiments: NonOpt-only (p. 14): 900 synthetic QPs built from prescribed solutions, DAS vs IPM CPU time by n, d* type and m (pp. 15-17); 20 scalable problems at n = 1000, three direction strategies, speed (~85 s total) vs accuracy (~580 s total) settings with iterations, evaluations, final f, CPU (pp. 19-20, Tables 2-3 pp. 26-27); 488,235-variable image denoising with four regularizers, parameters tuned against the clean image (pp. 20-22, Table 4 p. 27); single runs.
positioning: Self-lineage of codes from Matlab to SVANO to NonOpt; DAS generalizes Kiwiel; step sizes from his own Curtis-Nocedal 2007; default behaviour likened to Lewis-Overton BFGS; heuristic termination as in LMBM and HANSO (pp. 2, 9, 11-12, 18-19).
writing: User-manual register: per-module lists of most influential options with defaults; candid warnings about critical parameters and expensive cases; magic numbers attributed to extensive experimentation (pp. 7-9, 12, 14).
limits_future: Heuristic termination; m << n not covered by the QP study; expensive re-solves when the trust region binds at large n; no external comparison; ground-truth tuning in denoising; future work implied via extensibility and swappable linear algebra (pp. 3, 14, 17-18, 22).

method_links.note: QP solver tailored to the outer method: inexact termination tests from [7], IPM written for the specific dual, trust-region variables only when needed, DAS/IPM switch by size.
Strategies as interchangeable objects (direction, line search, QP solver, Hessian storage, termination); prints that the simplest gradient strategy is often fastest.
No external rival at all (justified by lack of maintained competitors); single runs; denoising parameters tuned on the ground truth (Tension 2).
Ideal stationarity test discussed as impractical; results judged by final f against known f*, not termination flags.
Constructed QP instances with known solutions (not infeasible/degenerate variants), with the uncovered case m << n stated.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Same 20-problem set run with speed and accuracy tolerances, total wall times (85 s vs 580 s) reported to show the price of digits.

transferable: Generate QP test instances backwards from a prescribed solution and KKT-consistent multipliers to control correctness and active-set difficulty (pp. 15-16).
In a software paper, document per module only the few options that most affect performance, with defaults (pp. 7-9).
Solve the reduced subproblem without rarely active constraints first and re-solve the full one only if the dropped constraint is violated (p. 14).
Run one test set under speed and accuracy settings and report total time for each (pp. 15, 20).

quotes.text: Perhaps the most challenging issue when it comes to the implementation of a general-purpose algorithm for locally Lipschitz minimization is selecting effective termination criteria.
However, since NonOpt performed favorably in these comparisons, LMBM is no longer under active development

title: Robust Server Defense Against Unreliable Clients in One-Shot Fair Collaborative Machine Learning
contribution: A bilevel server-side reweighting of client proxy data with fairness penalties and a tiny trusted root dataset (read as arXiv v1), which keeps group fairness when unreliable clients are the majority, where loss-based robust weighting fails.
problem_entry: One-shot collaborative learning removes iterative server correction; existing defenses are multi-round and assume unreliable clients are a minority (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Inner weighted logistic regression on proxy data, outer loss on a trusted root set with decision-boundary-covariance fairness constraints moved into penalties; hypergradients by implicit differentiation and simplex projection (pp. 4-5).
assumptions: Linear logistic model; binary sensitive attribute and labels; root dataset of about 0.5% drawn from each client's distribution (admitted limitation); DBC fairness surrogate; no theory (pp. 4-5, 8).
proof_devices: n/a (no theorems)
hypergradient through the inner Hessian linear system (13) (p. 5)
sort-based Euclidean projection onto the simplex, Algorithm 3 (p. 4)
experiments: Law School and Dutch, K = 5 clients, 20/40/60% unreliable, ideal and realistic scenarios, 5 seeds; accuracy, |SPD|, |EOD| on reliable clients' test data only; baselines unweighted, FedASL and FedNolowe adapted to one shot; fixed penalty schedule x10 every 400 iterations; fairness much better at 60% (e.g. 0.0403 vs 0.4948), rivals' higher accuracy printed, EO accuracy drop up to about 7 points (pp. 5-8).
positioning: Against multi-round robust aggregation, anomaly filtering and trust weighting (root-dataset idea credited to FLTrust-type work) and multi-round fairness-aware FL; builds on the authors' bilevel synthetic-data paper [3] (pp. 2-3, 6, 8).
writing: IEEE conference style with three bullet contributions; limitation sentence repeated verbatim; abstract's 'consistently outperforming' and 'little accuracy loss' framed on fairness while accuracy favours rivals (pp. 1-2, 4, 8).
limits_future: Root-dataset dependence, linear model, two datasets, five clients, no theory, fixed penalty schedule; no future directions (pp. 4, 6, 8).

method_links.note: Fairness constraints handled by a penalty raised on a fixed timetable (x10 every 400 iterations), the classical schedule Method 2 opposes (Tension 3).
Rivals adapted to the protocol with the adaptation described, same partitions, rivals' accuracy wins printed, rho_s = 0 ablation, 5-seed averages.
Scenarios constructed to break the rivals' majority assumption (60% unreliable) and an ideal scenario isolating the mechanism.
Evaluation on reliable clients only is justified openly, but the abstract's accuracy claim glosses over the EO accuracy drop.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Trusted audit set as outer objective
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A 0.5% trusted root dataset is the outer objective of a bilevel reweighting of untrusted client data.

transferable: Bilevel reweighting of untrusted data: inner weighted ERM, outer loss on a small trusted set, implicit-differentiation hypergradient, sort-based simplex projection (pp. 4-5).
In simulations, rank clients by their own metric to decide deterministically which are unreliable and push the unreliable fraction past 50% (p. 6).
Show learned weights in an idealized scenario as a mechanism check before headline metrics (p. 7).
Adapt rivals built for another protocol minimally, describe the adaptation and keep their published hyperparameters (p. 7).

quotes.text: This reliance on a root dataset is a limitation that may not be feasible in all scenarios.
This adaptation ensures a fair comparison under the one-shot communication constraint.
